clause: 4
4.3 Charpy V-notch impact test
Standard Charpy V-notch test specimens shall be prepared and tested as specified in DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.1
Sec.3.
The test specimens shall be cut with their longitudinal axis transverse to the weld length, with the notch
perpendicular to the surface of the plate and positioned as follows:
— for deposited metal and butt weld test assemblies with multi-run technique, the test specimens shall be
cut at mid thickness of the weld
— for two-run welded test assemblies the specimens shall be cut on the 2nd run side, 2 mm below the
surface
— for electroslag or electrogas welded test assemblies the specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the surface
and for test piece thicknesses above 20 mm additional test specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the root
side of the test assembly
— for one-side automatic welding processes, the test specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the face side and 2
mm below the root side of the test assembly.
The average absorbed energy value shall comply with the requirements of the applicable subsequent section.
One individual value may be less than the required average value provided that it is not less than 70% of this
value.

3 Testing procedure
The test welds shall normally be made on the materials listed in the rules DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.2 for which
approval of the welding consumable is desired. Any grade of structural steel (see DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.2
Sec.2) may be used for the preparation of the all-weld-metal test assemblies.
The test specimens shall be made under controlled conditions, on metal deposited from the filler metal in
question.
When a test weld is performed, the edges of the plates shall be bevelled either by mechanical machining or
by oxygen cutting, in the latter case, a descaling of the edges is necessary.
After being welded, the test assemblies shall not be subjected to any heat treatment.
If manufacturer request approval for the heat-treated condition, additional test pieces shall be prepared and
heat-treated accordingly.
It is recommended that the welded assembly is subjected to radiographic examination to ascertain whether
there are any defects in the weld prior to testing.

clause: 2
2.4 Environmental tests
Tests related to endurance and reliability of the product on board ships, e.g. vibration test, should take
account of the environmental strains on board vessels.
In case of insufficient experience from service on board ships (or equivalent), the following tests may be
required as type tests:
— vibration test according to DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.4 Ch.8 Electrical Installations and the Society's document
DNV-CG-0339 or IEC 60947-1 App.Q
— damp heat test, according to DNV-CG-0339 or IEC 60947-1 App.Q
— dry heat test, according to DNV-CG-0339 or IEC 60947-1 App.Q
— salt mist test according to DNV-CG-0339 or IEC 60947-1 App.Q (only applicable if a risk for exposure of
salty atmosphere)
— conducted emissions, according to DNV-CG-0339
— radiated emissions, according to DNV-CG-0339.
Conducted emissions and radiated emissions are only applicable for products equipped with electronic
devices. Alternatively to DNV-CG-0339, the requirements in the product standards may be followed.

1 Design requirements
The Low voltage switchgear and controlgear up to rated voltage 1000 V AC and 1500 V DC shall comply with
relevant requirements of publications in its latest edition, including amendments, as listed in Sec.1 Table 1
and Sec.1 Table 2.
Sec.1 Table 1 lists DNV standards general to all switchgear and controlgear. Sec.1 Table 2 refers to IEC
60947-1, applicable for all switchgear and controlgear, and specific standards for each type of switchgear and
controlgear.

gold_evidence.context:
Background
2
The report of the forty-seventh meeting of the GESAMP-Ballast Water Working Group
(GESAMP-BWWG) (MEPC 84/4/3) mentions in paragraph 3.2 that the Group initiated
discussions on topics listed in the agenda for its tenth stocktaking workshop. Time constraints
did not allow the Group to discuss all matters at the stocktaking workshop in detail, and it
agreed to revisit them at a future opportunity and submit its report to a future session. Given
this reality, and in order to contribute to the stocktaking exercise and the need for continued
research and monitoring of present and future ballast water management and impacts, this
document summarizes a recent report1 on ballast water operations, discharges and their
impacts in the Gulf of California (GoC) from future liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker traffic.
The majority of the findings in the report are based on a comprehensive review of scientific
literature. Modelling methodologies are summarized.

Report background
3
Increased LNG tanker traffic in the GoC introduces stressors like underwater radiated
noise (URN) and the risk of whale strikes, while invasive aquatic species can outcompete
native species, disrupt food webs, introduce pathogens, and alter habitats. Collectively, these
changes have the potential to adversely affect the marine environment, native and migratory
species, and nearby coastal communities through both direct and cumulative impacts.
4
Invasive
aquatic
species
impose
a
global
economic
cost
estimated
at 345 billion $USD/5.9 trillion MXN, with North America bearing nearly half (48%) of reported
invasion costs.2,3 From 1992 to 2019, aquatic and semi-aquatic invasive species cost Mexico
an estimated 4.16 billion USD/78.65 billion MXN, representing 78% of the total economic
damages caused by invasive species in the country during that period.4 Preventing introduction
is the most cost-effective strategy; once a species establishes and spreads, eradication
becomes nearly impossible and exponentially more expensive.
5
LNG tankers can operate on "single-stop" voyages, meaning they arrive at export
terminals effectively empty of cargo and thus under full ballast volumes to maintain stability.
The Saguaro LNG Phase 3 project is projected to involve the discharge of up to 30 million
metric tonnes (30 billion litres) of ballast water from tankers annually, if LNG tankers discharge
at each port call.

gold_evidence.context:
Mandate
3
The Technical Body will have within its mandate the following tasks:
(a)
review and formulate proposals for amendments to any: (i) technical clauses
of Tiers 2-3 of the CTU Code; and/or (ii) the content of the Supplement
included in Tier 4, without pre-empting, lowering, or contradicting any of the
principles contained in the chapters and ILO addendum of Tier 1;
(b)
submit amendment proposals to the clauses and contents of Tiers 2–3 and/or
Tier 4, for consideration by its parent body for approval in accordance with
the mandates and methods of work of the involved organizations;*
(c)
if adopted, prepare a publication of the changes and amendments to update
the relevant sections of Tiers 2–3 and/or Tier 4;
(d)
advise and update the parent body, when changes to clauses in Tier 1 are
identified as necessary, for the parent body to start an appropriate process
in accordance with the mandates and methods of work of the involved
organizations;
(e)
consider and prepare any processes for the parent body to decide on the
establishment of a funding mechanism to be entrusted to UNECE; and
(f)
report annually on its activities to the parent body, and share this information
with IMO and ILO.

Methods of work
7
The Technical Body is expected to meet at least once a year at the Palais des Nations
in Geneva and/or online in accordance with the ECE Guidelines. Each annual session should
be at least two days in length, but may be extended if circumstances require and resources
allow.
8
In addition to its annual meeting, special sessions may be requested if urgent matters
arise concerning technical clauses in Tiers 2–4 that may require additional time for
consideration.
9
The Technical Body may choose to set up informal or correspondence groups to
consider certain aspects of technical clauses, to support its analysis and decision-making
process. This would be on an ad hoc basis and not included in the otherwise provided budget
allocation. Secretariat services will not be provided by ECE for these informal groups.
